prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength concept and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep B019 first after reading all eight ballots. The optical lattice clock is a new measurement capability, not a refinement. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift to first order, so many atoms can be interrogated at once with long coherence times. Ye's group then pushed accuracy and stability to the 10^-18 level, with resolved systematic budgets and clock-clock comparisons. That gives a clean proposal-plus-realisation pair that fits two laureates. It is reproduced at JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB and NIST with agreed uncertainty budgets, and it is already used for relativistic geodesy, constraints on constant variation and the preparation for redefining the second. Four colleagues (Lindroth, Pearce, Olsson, Mehlig) also ranked it and all five proposals name the same pair, so the attribution question looks settled as far as the supplied names go. Few candidates combine this much experimental evidence, reproducibility and demonstrated reach beyond the field.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap and incrementalism. The frequency comb (Hall and Hänsch, 2005) and ion trapping and cooling (Wineland, 2012) already honoured the toolbox, so a committee could read lattice clocks as a long, steady improvement in precision without a single decisive discovery. The credit is also not airtight, since Lemonde, Derevianko on the theory side, and ion-clock groups with competing accuracy records are not named. Finally, only three of eight members put it first, and Johansson, Eriksson and Danielsson did not rank it at all, so its breadth of support is narrower than B047 or B017.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B019 only sixth because it is close in spirit to the earlier metrology prizes and may be a long incremental improvement rather than a single discovery.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously but disagree on the incrementalism. The comb is a ruler for optical frequencies; the lattice clock is a different object, because the magic wavelength is what lets millions of atoms be probed without Doppler or light-shift penalty, and that is why the accuracy moved from 10^-16 to 10^-18 and the many-body clock became possible. A statistical gain from N atoms combined with a vanishing systematic is a qualitative change, and the 2012 prize for single ions did not cover it. I do accept that the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly so the comb overlap is not an issue.

responses.point: Olsson put B047 first, praising the theory-then-experiment story and the breadth of the moire materials field, and ranked B019 fourth.
responses.response: I agree that magic-angle graphene has had enormous follow-on, and that Bistritzer-MacDonald is the kind of prediction I respect. My reservation is maturity and reproducibility. Several colleagues, Eriksson, Johansson and you, note that the superconducting mechanism is unsettled, and twist-angle disorder and sample-to-sample variation still limit quantitative comparison. I also worry about the experimental credit, since Cao and Fatemi did the 2018 measurements and are outside the three names. For the lattice clock the accuracy budgets are stated and independently checked, so the claim being rewarded is not in doubt. I would not oppose B047 later, but I think it benefits from a few more years.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B004) first as the standard architecture for superconducting qubits, with strong reproducibility and a natural link to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I ranked B004 fifth and I think the point of difference is what is being rewarded. The strong-coupling physics of Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is real, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits has just honoured the superconducting-circuit platform, and the transmon, Devoret and Girvin credit questions are not resolved by the three names. I would not call that a fatal flaw, but it makes a follow-up in the same year less compelling to me than a result from a different area. If the committee wants a quantum-technology prize, I would find B004 easier to defend than colleagues who prefer solid-state spin candidates.

responses.point: Lindroth also ranked B019 first, stressing tests of fundamental constants and the clean idea, while listing overlap with 2005 and 2012 and uncited theory contributions as uncertainties.
responses.response: I agree with your framing and with the pair. On the uncited theory, I would not extend the prize to Derevianko or Lemonde: the decisive step is the experimental demonstration that the magic-wavelength condition works and then yields 10^-18, which is exactly what Katori and Ye did. I would ask the committee to check the priority of the early Sr lattice-clock measurements at Tokyo, JILA and SYRTE in the supporting record, since that is where a dispute could arise.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranked B019 first on calibration and systematics grounds and considered the Katori-Ye allocation fair.
responses.response: I agree and would add that the evidence for the systematic budgets is the best argument for maturity: they have been reproduced through international clock comparisons, not only by the originating groups. I would qualify one point. Your argument that the work is lasting rests on the planned redefinition of the second, but that is a decision outside physics and should not carry weight in the scientific case. The case must stand on the magic-wavelength concept and the 10^-18 demonstration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as an incremental extension of the frequency comb and ion-clock prizes.
Priority between Katori's group, the JILA group and the SYRTE group for the first Sr lattice clock, and whether Lemonde or Derevianko should be recognised.
Whether a second, quantum-simulation part could be added (B017), which is not possible within the three-person limit without dropping a laureate.
I rely on recall for dates and accuracy numbers, not on a verified source.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B019 is apparent from my profile. One connection to note: I am part of the WACQT management team (Chalmers-led), which overlaps institutionally with Göran Johansson's home institution and with the superconducting-circuit work behind B004, so I would recuse myself on B004 if it advanced. I also work on rare-earth-ion quantum memories and am on the management team of Deep Light Vision, which concern none of the shortlisted candidates directly.
